title: Reconceptualizing Prenatal Sex Steroids in Autism: A Toxicological Critique of the Baron-Cohen Framework
content: Professor Sir Simon Baron-Cohen’s public acknowledgment that the phrase “extreme male brain” is clinically unhelpful marks a critical juncture for neurodevelopmental psychiatry. However, mainstream models continue to attribute the primary etiology of autism to hardwired genetic determinism. This opinion presents an alternative systems-biology framework: prenatal steroid profiles are indicators of a reactive maternal-fetal endocrine triage prioritizing pregnancy viability under severe environmental stress. We mechanically model how ambient nitrous oxide (N₂O) exposure passivates cobalamin and paralyzes mitochondrial clearance lanes, forcing an explosive maternal neuroendocrine rebound that drives an influx of sex steroids into the amniotic space. Crucially, we demonstrate that the "missing heritability" paradox is an analytical artifact manufactured by a systemic violation of the Equal Environments Assumption (EEA). By mapping human gestational plumbing—specifically monochorionic synchrony versus dichorionic asymmetric filtering—we prove that blood-borne exposures are distributed unevenly. Pushing these anatomical variables to their boundaries reveals a complete algorithmic model collapse within Falconer’s formula, generating an impossible heritability artifact (120.6%). We detail how direct molecular pipelines (GWAS) automatically discard these structural somatic duplications as noise, while twin registries mislabel synchronized in utero shocks as genetic inheritance. Phenotypic resolution is determined by sex-divergent fetal utilization: while the female fetus leverages a cell-autonomous buffer and an ERβ-driven methylation pump, the male fetus faces structural vulnerability via metabotropic networks. Within this paradigm, post-natal neurobehavioral traits represent a homeostatic kappa opioid receptor protective shield deployed against a gestational bioenergetic crisis, providing a quantifiable structural correction to behavioral genetic models.
